claim: Motor control, motor learning, self-recognition, and spatial perception all critically depend on the comparison of motor intention to the actually executed movement.
source: Motor control, motor learning, self-recognition, and spatial perception all critically depend on the comparison of motor intention to the actually executed movement.
evidence: This is a general statement about motor control that draws from established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: The brainstem-cerebellum plays an important role in motor error detection and motor learning.
source: Despite our knowledge that the brainstem-cerebellum plays an important role in motor error detection and motor learning, the involvement of neocortex remains largely unclear.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge in the field about brainstem-cerebellum function.

claim: The involvement of neocortex in motor error detection and motor learning remains largely unclear.
source: Despite our knowledge that the brainstem-cerebellum plays an important role in motor error detection and motor learning, the involvement of neocortex remains largely unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: PPS neurons in macaque posterior parietal cortex represent the intended end-position of saccade.
source: Neurons with persistent pre- and post-saccadic response (PPS) represent the intended end-position of saccade
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation patterns between PPS neuron activity and saccade parameters.

claim: LPS neurons in macaque posterior parietal cortex represent the actual end-position of saccade.
source: neurons with late post-saccadic response (LPS) represent the actual end-position of saccade.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing correlation between LPS neuron activity and actual saccade end-positions.

claim: After the arrival of the LPS signal, the PPS neurons' activity becomes highly correlated with the discrepancy between intended and actual end-position.
source: Remarkably, after the arrival of the LPS signal, the PPS neurons' activity becomes highly correlated with the discrepancy between intended and actual end-position, and with the probability of making secondary (corrective) saccades.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses presented in the manuscript showing relationships between PPS activity and saccadic error.

claim: PPS neurons' activity after the arrival of the LPS signal is correlated with the probability of making secondary (corrective) saccades.
source: Remarkably, after the arrival of the LPS signal, the PPS neurons' activity becomes highly correlated with the discrepancy between intended and actual end-position, and with the probability of making secondary (corrective) saccades.
evidence: This is supported by data showing correlation between post-subtraction activity and secondary saccade probability.

claim: Executed actions are not always perfectly matched with intended ones, but have errors, even for very well trained actions.
source: However, a noticeable fact is that the executed actions are not always perfectly matched with the intended (desired) ones, but have errors. This is true even for very well trained actions (Shadmehr et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The brain must evolve efficient mechanisms to detect motor errors between intended and executed actions for motor control, motor learning, spatial perception, and other motor-related cognitive functions.
source: Therefore, the brain must evolve efficient mechanisms to detect the motor errors between the intended and the executed actions for motor control, motor learning, spatial perception, and other motor-related cognitive functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that motor errors occur and need to be corrected.

claim: Executed motor actions can be encoded by internal movement-related signals (e.g., efference copy/corollary discharge).
source: The executed motor actions can be encoded by two types of signals in the brain: the internal movement-related signals (e.g., efference copy/corollary discharge) (Helmholtz, 1925; Sherrington, 1918) and the external sensory signals (e.g., proprioception) (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: Executed motor actions can be encoded by external sensory signals (e.g., proprioception).
source: The executed motor actions can be encoded by two types of signals in the brain: the internal movement-related signals (e.g., efference copy/corollary discharge) (Helmholtz, 1925; Sherrington, 1918) and the external sensory signals (e.g., proprioception) (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In self-originated movements, internal signals predict the displacement of motor effector.
source: In self-originated movements, the internal signals predict the displacement of motor effector (Crapse and Sommer, 2008; Duhamel et al., 1992; Helmholtz, 1925; Sommer and Wurtz, 2002; Sperry, 1950)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: External sensory signals inform the actual position of the motor effector.
source: whereas the external sensory signals inform its actual position (Fuchs and Kornhuber, 1969; Sherrington, 1918).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The emergence of sensory information lags the execution of movement.
source: Because the emergence of the sensory information lags the execution of the movement, it is believed that the motor errors in high velocity movements, such as saccades, are calculated by relying heavily on the internal signals (Kawato, 1999; Robinson, 1975; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2010; Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sensory processing delays.

claim: Motor errors in high velocity movements, such as saccades, are calculated by relying heavily on internal signals.
source: Because the emergence of the sensory information lags the execution of the movement, it is believed that the motor errors in high velocity movements, such as saccades, are calculated by relying heavily on the internal signals (Kawato, 1999; Robinson, 1975; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2010; Wolpert et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Online control of saccades and saccadic learning can be fully explained by models reflecting the properties of the brainstem-cerebellum machinery for saccades.
source: Over the past three decades, the online control of saccades as well as saccadic learning can, in principle, be fully explained by the well-established models that reflect the properties of the brainstem-cerebellum machinery for saccades (Barash et al., 1999; Catz et al., 2005; Dash and Thier, 2014; Ito, 1970; Kawato et al., 2003; Nowak et al., 2007; Pasalar et al., 2006; Robinson, 1975; Shadmehr and Krakauer, 2008; Shadmehr et al., 2010; Stein, 2009; Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior modeling and experimental work.

claim: Whether neocortex is involved in saccadic error detection is largely unknown.
source: However, up to date, whether neocortex is also involved in saccadic error detection is largely unknown.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: 753 neurons were recorded in total from macaque posterior parietal cortex.
source: In total, we recorded 753 neurons, in which 377 out of 753 neurons showed significant pre-saccadic activity (pre-saccadic neurons) whereas 107 neurons showed significant pure post-saccadic activity (post-saccadic neurons).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data collection.

claim: 377 out of 753 neurons showed significant pre-saccadic activity.
source: In total, we recorded 753 neurons, in which 377 out of 753 neurons showed significant pre-saccadic activity (pre-saccadic neurons) whereas 107 neurons showed significant pure post-saccadic activity (post-saccadic neurons).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: 107 neurons showed significant pure post-saccadic activity.
source: In total, we recorded 753 neurons, in which 377 out of 753 neurons showed significant pre-saccadic activity (pre-saccadic neurons) whereas 107 neurons showed significant pure post-saccadic activity (post-saccadic neurons).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: All neurons but one were recorded within a small area of 3x4 mm2 in monkey B and 3x3 mm2 in monkey D.
source: The reconstructed recording sites show that all neurons, but one, were recorded within a small area of 3x4 mm2 in monkey B and 3x3 mm2 in monkey D.
evidence: This is a direct report of recording site reconstruction data.

claim: The neurons shown in this study were probably recorded mostly from the lateral intraparietal area (LIP).
source: Therefore, the neurons shown in this study were probably recorded mostly from the LIP.
evidence: This is an inference based on recording locations and physiological signatures.

claim: 89 out of 377 pre-saccadic neurons discharged persistently in both pre- and post-saccadic intervals (PPS neurons).
source: We identified a group of pre-saccadic response neurons (89 out of 377) that discharged persistently in both pre- and post-saccadic intervals (PPS) when saccades were directed to the response fields (preferred direction).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data classification.

claim: 27 neurons were identified with late post-saccadic responses (LPS).
source: We also identified another 27 neurons with late post-saccadic responses (LPS).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data classification.

claim: The activity of PPS neurons started to decay at ~74.8 ms (STD = 33.1) after the completion of the saccade.
source: On average, the activity of PPS neurons started to decay at ~74.8 ms (STD = 33.1) after the completion of the saccade.
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative analysis of neuronal activity timing.

claim: All but seven PPS neurons had significantly higher pre-saccadic activity in the preferred direction than in the non-preferred direction.
source: All but seven neurons had significantly higher activity (p<0.05, Wilcoxon test) in the preferred direction than in the non-preferred one.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The pre-saccadic and early post-saccadic activities of PPS neurons were significantly and positively correlated in 34 of 89 neurons.
source: The results show that the pre-saccadic and the early post-saccadic activities were significantly and positively correlated in 34 of 89 neurons (p<0.05, t-test), and this correlation was also observed in the population data (mean r = 0.2151, p<0.001, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The correlation coefficient values of 55 PPS neurons between perisaccadic activity and saccade end-position were symmetrically distributed around zero (mean r = 0.0132, p=0.5242).
source: Overall, the correlation coefficient values of these 55 PPS neurons were symmetrically distributed around zero (Figure 2D, mean r = 0.0132, p=0.5242, paired t-test), suggesting that their responses are not directly encoding the actual end-position of saccades.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons does not encode the actual end-position of saccades.
source: These results indicated that the perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons does not likely encode the actual end-position of saccades.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between PPS activity and actual saccade end-positions.

claim: The same PPS neurons were not visually responsive during the visual feedback after finishing saccades in the MGS task.
source: However, we found that during the MGS task, the same PPS neurons were not visually responsive during the visual feedback after finishing saccades (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The absence of a visual response during the MGS feedback stimulus suggests that the perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons was not a foveal visual response.
source: The absence of a visual response during the MGS feedback stimulus suggests that the perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons was not a foveal visual response.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of visual response in the MGS task.

claim: The absolute firing rate of PPS neurons was significantly higher in the SCS task than in the MGS task.
source: While the absolute firing rate was significantly higher in the SCS task than that in the MGS task (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, in population level, p<0.001, paired t-test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The relative change in activity of PPS neurons was very similar between SCS and MGS tasks.
source: the relative change in activity, comparing the perisaccadic interval (-150~100 ms of saccade end) with the interval of 100~300 ms before saccade onset, was very similar between two tasks (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D, in population level, p=0.2887, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4D.

claim: The intended end-position is encoded by the relative change, rather than the absolute firing rate, of the perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons.
source: Such results suggested that the intended end-position was not task specific and it might be more reliably encoded by the relative change of activity of PPS neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of activity patterns across tasks.

claim: LPS neurons started to discharge with a mean delay of 70.9 ms (STD = 31.3 ms) after saccade completion.
source: In addition to the PPS neurons, we also recorded a group of neurons which started to discharge with a relatively long delay after saccade completion (LPS neurons, mean = 70.9 ms, STD = 31.3 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of quantitative analysis of neuronal activity timing.

claim: All but two LPS neurons showed stronger post-saccadic activities in one direction than in the other.
source: Comparing the post-saccadic activities (25~225 ms after saccade end) of individual LPS neurons between trials in which saccades were directed to the opposite directions, all but two LPS neurons showed stronger activities in one direction than in the other (Figure 3C, p<0.05, Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The distribution of correlation coefficient values of 22 LPS neurons was significantly biased to the positive direction (mean r = 0.1237, p=0.0074).
source: Indeed, we found that the distribution of the correlation coefficient values of these 22 LPS neurons was significantly biased to the positive direction (Figure 3D, mean r = 0.1237, p=0.0074, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 18 out of 22 LPS neurons tended to be positively correlated with the end-position of saccades, with 5 reaching statistical significance.
source: On a single neuron basis, we found that 18 out of 22 LPS neurons tended to be positively correlated with the end-position of saccades, with 5 reaching statistical significance (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The activity of LPS neurons was positively correlated with the actual end-position of saccades.
source: Taken together, although subject to noise on a single neuron basis, our results show that, in contrast to the PPS neurons, the activity of LPS neurons was positively correlated with the actual end-position of saccades.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Both the absolute firing rate and the relative change of the normalized post-saccadic activity of LPS neurons were similar between SCS and MGS tasks.
source: Both the absolute firing rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, in population, p=0.6526, paired t-test) and the relative change of the normalized post-saccadic activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, in population, p=0.7262, paired t-test) were similar between the two tasks.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The LPS neurons started to increase their activity 25 ms before the decay of PPS neurons.
source: On average, the LPS neurons started to increase their activity 25 ms before the decay of PPS neurons, indicating the temporal overlap of the PPS and LPS signals in PPC.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the temporal characteristics of neuronal activity.

claim: There is temporal overlap of the PPS and LPS signals in PPC.
source: On average, the LPS neurons started to increase their activity 25 ms before the decay of PPS neurons, indicating the temporal overlap of the PPS and LPS signals in PPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing analysis of neuronal activities.

claim: The averaged post-saccadic activity of LPS neurons was positively correlated with the end-position of saccade (r = 0.9791, p=0.0006).
source: The averaged post-saccadic activity (25~125 ms after saccade end) of the LPS neurons was positively correlated with the end-position of saccade (Figure 4D, red, r = 0.9791, p=0.0006, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons did not vary among different end-positions of saccades (r = -0.1355, p=0.6168).
source: In contrast, the perisaccadic activity of PPS neurons (-150~100 ms to saccade end) did not vary among different end-positions of saccades (Figure 4D, black, r = -0.1355, p=0.6168, t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The farther away the end-position of saccades is from the location of saccadic target, the higher the activity of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval.
source: However, shortly after the arrival of the late post-saccadic activity of LPS neurons (150–350 ms after saccade end), the discharge level of the PPS neurons varied among different subsets of trials (Figure 4C, within solid rectangle); that is, the farther away the end-position of saccades is from the location of saccadic target, the higher the activity of PPS neurons.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neuronal activity patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 43 out of 55 PPS neurons showed positive correlation between activity and magnitude of saccadic error, with 19 reaching statistical significance.
source: While 12 out of 55 PPS neurons showed negative correlation (2 neurons reached statistically significant level), 43 out of 55 neurons showed positive correlation, and 19 neurons reached statistically significant level (p<0.05, t-test).
evidence: This is a direct report of statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The population correlation data showed a significant positive correlation between PPS neuron activity and magnitude of saccadic error (mean r = 0.155, p<0.0001).
source: Overall, the population correlation data showed a significant positive correlation with the magnitude of saccadic error (Figure 4F, mean r = 0.155, p<0.0001, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The absolute difference between the two regression fittings of normalized activities of PPS and LPS neurons overlapped with the activity of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval.
source: Consistent with the subtraction model, the absolute difference between the two regression fittings of normalized activities of PPS and LPS neurons (Figure 4G, purple dashed lines) clearly overlapped with the activity of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval (150–350 ms after saccade end) (Figure 4G, black lines).
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The correlation between population activities of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval and magnitude of saccadic errors was significantly higher than the correlation with end-position of saccade.
source: Moreover, the correlation between population activities of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval and the magnitude of saccadic errors was significantly higher (p=0.0314, paired t-test) than the correlation with the end-position of saccade (mean r = 0.1134).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: The correlation between population activities of PPS neurons in the late post-saccadic interval and magnitude of saccadic errors was significantly higher than the correlation with saccade amplitude.
source: It was also significantly higher (p=0.0023, paired t-test) than the correlation with the saccade amplitude (mean r = 0.0898).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: The level of post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons was correlated positively with the discrepancy (error) between the intended and actual end-position of saccade.
source: Thus, the level of the post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons was correlated positively with the discrepancy (error) between the intended (target location) and the actual end-position of saccade.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The post-subtraction activity did not differentiate whether the error was from a hypometric or a hypermetric saccade.
source: However, the post-subtraction activity did not differentiate whether the error was from a hypometric or a hypermetric saccade.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the parabolic distribution of activity with respect to saccade error.

claim: The population post-subtraction activity showed significant positive correlation with saccade error in a relatively long interval (120–380 ms after saccade end).
source: As shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, the population post-subtraction activity showed significant positive correlation with saccade error in a relatively long interval (120–380 ms after saccade end).
evidence: This is supported by sliding window analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: During 150–300 ms after saccade end, the correlation between post-subtraction activity and saccade error was significantly positive (mean r > 0.1) and stable.
source: In particular, during 150–300 ms the correlation was significantly positive (mean r > 0.1) and stable.
evidence: This is based on sliding window analysis of correlation over time.

claim: PPS neurons might estimate the congruence between intended and actual end-position of saccades through subtracting the actual signal from intention signal.
source: Therefore, our results suggested that the PPS neurons might estimate the congruence between intended and actual end-position of saccades through subtracting the actual signal from intention signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the match between subtraction model predictions and experimental data.

claim: In 1009 out of 4090 trials, the monkeys made a secondary (corrective) saccade following the primary saccade.
source: In 1009 out of 4090 trials, the monkeys made a secondary (corrective) saccade following the primary saccade.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: The majority of secondary saccades (851 of 1009) were directed toward the saccade target.
source: The majority of the secondary saccades (851 of 1009) were directed toward the saccade target.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data.

claim: The probability of making a secondary saccade was reduced following the reduction of the primary saccadic error.
source: We found that the probability of making a secondary saccade was reduced following the reduction of the primary saccadic error (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons was positively correlated with the probability of making a secondary saccade (r = 0.8289, p=0.0001).
source: Also, the post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons was positively correlated with the probability of making a secondary saccade (Figure 5B, r = 0.8289, p=0.0001 t-test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The post-subtraction activity was significantly higher in trials with a secondary saccade compared to trials without a secondary saccade.
source: Furthermore, when comparing trials with and without a secondary saccade, the post-subtraction activity was significantly higher in the trials with a secondary saccade (Figure 5C and Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The distributions of PPS and LPS neurons largely overlapped in both monkeys.
source: Data showed that the distributions of the PPS and LPS neurons largely overlapped in both monkeys.
evidence: This is based on reconstruction of recording sites shown in Figure 6.

claim: The intermingled distributions of PPS and LPS neurons indicate that they were recorded from the same area of PPC.
source: Such intermingled distributions of PPS and LPS neurons indicated that PPS and LPS were recorded from the same area of PPC, suggesting the functional interaction between the two types of neurons is possible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of recorded neurons.

claim: Functional interaction between PPS and LPS neurons is possible.
source: Such intermingled distributions of PPS and LPS neurons indicated that PPS and LPS were recorded from the same area of PPC, suggesting the functional interaction between the two types of neurons is possible.
evidence: This is speculation based on the anatomical proximity of the two neuron types.

claim: The end-positions of saccades for rewarded trials were distributed closely around the target as a Gaussian-like distribution with STD = 0.49°.
source: More importantly, the end-positions of saccades for rewarded trials were distributed closely around the target as a Gaussian-like distribution with STD = 0.49°.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data analysis.

claim: It is reasonable to assume that monkeys intended to make saccades to the target location.
source: Thus, it is reasonable to assume that monkeys did intend to make saccades to the target location.
evidence: This is an inference based on the training protocol and behavioral performance.

claim: The temporal profile of LPS activity is very similar to the extraocular proprioceptive response reported previously.
source: In contrast, the temporal profile of this LPS activity is very similar to the extraocular proprioceptive response reported previously (Prevosto et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior research findings cited in the text.

claim: The activity of LPS neurons represents more likely the extraocular proprioceptive signal rather than the visual signal.
source: Moreover, for the following reasons, we believe that the activity of LPS neurons represents more likely the extraocular proprioceptive signal rather than the visual signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including timing and lack of visual responses.

claim: The LPS neurons did not have visual responses in all three oculomotor tasks.
source: Firstly, the LPS neurons did not have visual responses in all three oculomotor tasks.
evidence: This is based on analysis of neuronal responses across different task conditions.

claim: The extraocular proprioceptive signal rose up in the primary somatosensory cortex ~30 ms after the end of saccade.
source: Thirdly, we previously reported that the extraocular proprioceptive signal rose up in the primary somatosensory cortex ~30 ms after the end of saccade (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This refers to prior research by the authors.

claim: The LPS neurons might encode an extraocular proprioceptive signal.
source: In our case, the LPS neurons started to discharge ~70 ms after saccade (Figure 4A–B), indicating that the LPS neurons might encode an extraocular proprioceptive signal (Genovesio et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on timing considerations and comparison with prior work.

claim: PPC is not directly involved in the control of saccadic eye movement.
source: Considering the fact that PPC is not directly involved in the control of saccadic eye movement (Li et al., 1999; Thier and Andersen, 1998; Wardak et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The saccadic error signal in PPC might function differently from the error signal that drives the premotor circuitry for saccade in the brainstem.
source: Considering the fact that PPC is not directly involved in the control of saccadic eye movement (Li et al., 1999; Thier and Andersen, 1998; Wardak et al., 2002), the saccadic error signal in PPC might function differently from the error signal that drives the premotor circuitry for saccade in the brainstem.
evidence: This is speculation based on anatomical and functional considerations.

claim: One possible function of the parietal error signal may be the programming of a secondary saccade in case of the primary saccade missing the target.
source: One possible function may be the programming of a secondary saccade in case of the primary saccade missing the target.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the observed signals.

claim: The comparison between the intended and actual end-position of saccade starts in PPC ~70 ms after the end of the primary saccade.
source: Our data show that the comparison between the intended and the actual end-position of saccade starts in PPC ~70 ms after the end of the primary saccade (Figure 4A–C), which is too late to influence the primary saccade but is early enough to control the secondary saccade (the latter has a latency of ~154 ms in average).
evidence: This is based on timing analysis of neuronal activity shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The timing of the comparison signal is too late to influence the primary saccade but is early enough to control the secondary saccade.
source: Our data show that the comparison between the intended and the actual end-position of saccade starts in PPC ~70 ms after the end of the primary saccade (Figure 4A–C), which is too late to influence the primary saccade but is early enough to control the secondary saccade (the latter has a latency of ~154 ms in average).
evidence: This is an inference based on timing considerations.

claim: The parietal error signal may reflect the programming of a secondary saccade, as suggested by the correlation between secondary saccade probability and post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons.
source: Therefore, this parietal error signal may reflect the next of programming a secondary saccade, a possibility that is suggested by the correlation between secondary saccade probability and the post-subtraction activity of PPS neurons.
evidence: This is speculation supported by correlation data.

claim: The brainstem-cerebellum models do not explain how a secondary saccade is planned.
source: In contrast, the brainstem-cerebellum models do not explain how a secondary saccade is planned.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of existing models.

claim: Short-term saccadic adaptation may be fully explained by the brainstem-cerebellum machinery.
source: The widely studied short-term saccadic adaptation may be fully explained by the brainstem-cerebellum machinery.
evidence: This is a statement about current understanding in the field.

claim: In parallel to short-term adaptation, a long-term adaptation (i.e., the post-adaptation effect lasting for days) is present.
source: In parallel to short-term adaptation, a long-term adaptation (i.e., the post-adaptation effect lasting for days) is present (Barash et al., 1999; Robinson et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neural basis for long-term adaptations remains unclear.
source: In parallel to short-term adaptation, a long-term adaptation (i.e., the post-adaptation effect lasting for days) is present (Barash et al., 1999; Robinson et al., 2006), and the neural basis for the long-term adaptations remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: There is evidence for meta-learning, that is, short-term adaptation becoming more rapid with repeated training.
source: There is evidence for meta-learning, that is, short-term adaptation becoming more rapid with repeated training (Kojima et al., 2004; Wong and Shelhamer, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are contentions of 'cognitive' modulation of short-term saccadic adaptation.
source: there are even contentions of 'cognitive' modulation of short-term saccadic adaptation (Cotti et al., 2009; Srimal and Curtis, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The cortical error representation observed in the present study may have to do with long-term adaptation, meta-learning, or cognitive modulation of adaptation.
source: The cortical error representation observed in the present study may have to do with any of these processes.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential functional significance of the findings.

claim: A saccade can be elicited either by the sudden appearance of an external stimulus (reactive saccade) or by an endogenous cue (voluntary saccade).
source: Another phenomenon is that a saccade can be elicited either by the sudden appearance of an external stimulus (reactive saccade) or by an endogenous cue (voluntary saccade).
evidence: This is established knowledge about saccade types.

claim: The saccadic adaptation of reactive and voluntary saccades involves different mechanisms and partially separated neural circuitries.
source: The cumulative evidence has shown that the saccadic adaptation of reactive and voluntary saccades involves different mechanisms and partially separated neural circuitries (Cotti et al., 2009; Deubel, 1995; Erkelens and Hulleman, 1993; Gaveau et al., 2005; Hopp and Fuchs, 2010; Panouilleres et al., 2014; Zimmermann and Lappe, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The brainstem-cerebellum circuitry plays a crucial role in the adaptation of reactive saccades.
source: While the brainstem-cerebellum circuitry plays a crucial role in the adaptation of reactive saccades (Barash et al., 1999; Hopp and Fuchs, 2004; Optican and Robinson, 1980; Panouilleres et al., 2015; Robinson et al., 2002; Takagi et al., 1998)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: PPC is highly involved in the adaptation of voluntary saccade.
source: PPC is highly involved in the adaptation of voluntary saccade (Gerardin et al., 2012; Panouilleres et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The parietal error signal found in the present study might contribute to the adaptation of voluntary saccades.
source: The parietal error signal found in the present study might contribute to the latter.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of the findings.

claim: Comparison between motor intention and proprioception is critical for motor learning.
source: Recent studies have shown that comparison between motor intention and proprioception is critical for motor learning (Desmurget and Grafton, 2000; Panouilleres et al., 2015; Wolpert et al., 2011; Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Comparison between motor intention and proprioception is critical for motor-related cognitive functions, such as motor awareness and self-recognition.
source: Recent studies have shown that comparison between motor intention and proprioception is critical for motor learning (Desmurget and Grafton, 2000; Panouilleres et al., 2015; Wolpert et al., 2011; Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000) and motor-related cognitive functions, such as motor awareness (Berti and Pia, 2006; Fink et al., 1999; Haggard, 2005) and self-recognition (Haggard, 2008; Jeannerod, 2003; Knoblich, 2002; van den Bos and Jeannerod, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: PPC of primates plays an important role in the comparison between motor intention and proprioception.
source: A line of evidence suggests that PPC of primates plays an important role in the comparison between motor intention and proprioception (Gerardin et al., 2012; Panouilleres et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patients with lesions in PPC frequently exhibit difficulties in evaluating and comparing the intended and actual positions for awareness of self-movement.
source: Clinical studies also found that patients with lesions in PPC frequently exhibit difficulties in evaluating and comparing the intended and actual positions for awareness of self-movement (Haarmeier et al., 1997; Sirigu et al., 1999)
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Patients with lesions in PPC have difficulties in maintaining and updating an internal representation of action state.
source: Clinical studies also found that patients with lesions in PPC frequently exhibit difficulties in evaluating and comparing the intended and actual positions for awareness of self-movement (Haarmeier et al., 1997; Sirigu et al., 1999), for maintaining and updating an internal representation of action state (Kawato and Wolpert, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Patients with lesions in PPC have difficulties in motor error correction.
source: Clinical studies also found that patients with lesions in PPC frequently exhibit difficulties in evaluating and comparing the intended and actual positions for awareness of self-movement (Haarmeier et al., 1997; Sirigu et al., 1999), for maintaining and updating an internal representation of action state (Kawato and Wolpert, 1998), and for motor error correction (Pisella et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: This study adds neuronal evidence for motor error computation in PPC.
source: Here, our study adds the neuronal evidence for motor error computation in PPC.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the current study.
